reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A rare multisystem autosomal recessive disorder defined by the triad of arthrogryposis, renal tubular dysfunction and cholestasis
The cholestasis characteristically occurs with normal or only mildly raised gamma-glutamyl transferase, an important diagnostic clue
Renal involvement is a proximal (and sometimes distal) renal tubular dysfunction with a Fanconi-like picture
Additional features include failure to thrive, ichthyosis, recurrent infections, platelet dysfunction and a bleeding tendency, and central nervous system malformations
Caused by variants in VPS33B or its partner VIPAS39, which are required for intracellular vesicle trafficking and cell polarity
Liver biopsy carries a serious bleeding risk owing to platelet dysfunction and should be approached with great caution
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, addressing cholestasis, electrolyte losses, nutrition and bleeding risk
reference.pathophysiology: ARC syndrome is caused by recessive loss-of-function variants in VPS33B or VIPAS39 (VPS16B), proteins that form a complex regulating the fusion and trafficking of intracellular vesicles and the establishment of apical-basolateral cell polarity. Disrupted trafficking impairs the correct positioning of membrane transporters and secretory machinery in epithelial cells, producing bile canalicular dysfunction (low-GGT cholestasis), renal tubular transport defects, and abnormal platelet alpha-granule content with consequent bleeding tendency. The trafficking defect during development, together with reduced foetal movement, also contributes to the joint contractures (arthrogryposis), giving the characteristic multisystem triad.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of neonatal cholestasis and biliary atresia
Cystinosis and other causes of the renal Fanconi syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests showing cholestasis with characteristically normal or low GGT
Renal tubular function assessment (electrolytes, acidosis, glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia)
Molecular genetic testing for VPS33B and VIPAS39
Platelet studies and coagulation assessment before any invasive procedure
Skin examination and biopsy for ichthyosis where needed
Neuroimaging for associated central nervous system malformation
redFlags: Bleeding, especially after biopsy or surgery, from platelet dysfunction
Severe electrolyte and acid-base disturbance from renal tubular losses
Failure to thrive and recurrent serious infection
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is poor, with most affected infants dying in the first year of life from infection, dehydration, bleeding or liver failure; some milder variants survive longer, and care is supportive rather than curative.
pitfalls: Performing a liver biopsy without recognising the high bleeding risk from platelet dysfunction
Overlooking the diagnostic clue of low-GGT cholestasis
Missing the renal tubular losses and undertreating electrolyte disturbance
Attributing the contractures to isolated arthrogryposis and failing to look for the multisystem features
